8a(1).fact: Opening the valve wide before ignition allows heavy propane gas to pool around the burner, creating a dangerous flare-up when the flame catches.
8a(1).misconception: Opening the fuel valve completely before striking a spark produces a faster, safer ignition.
8a(1).pamphlet_summary: Scouts operate pressurized canister stoves on a level ground surface after inspecting the rubber O-ring gasket for cracks or dirt. Lighting requires holding a lit match or spark igniter above the burner head before cracking the fuel valve open slightly (p. 58).
8a(1).socratic_question: Why should you hold your flame next to the burner head before turning the control valve?

8a(2).fact: Leaving an empty headspace inside the fuel tank is necessary because air must compress to build adequate operating pressure.
8a(2).misconception: Filling the fuel tank completely to the rim provides longer burn times without affecting stove performance.
8a(2).pamphlet_summary: Liquid fuel stoves require white gas poured through a filtered funnel into the tank, leaving an air pocket for pressurization. Pumping the plunger builds tank pressure, while preheating the generator tube vaporizes liquid fuel into a clean blue flame (p. 59).
8a(2).socratic_question: What physical change must happen to liquid white gas inside the generator tube before it can burn as a steady blue flame?

8a(3).fact: Fuel containers stored inside living shelters can leak volatile fumes that create severe fire and asphyxiation hazards in enclosed spaces.
8a(3).misconception: Storing fuel bottles and gas canisters inside a sleeping tent protects them from overnight freezing.
8a(3).pamphlet_summary: Campers store liquid fuel in designated metal bottles with child-resistant caps and secure gas canisters in upright, shaded positions away from heat sources. All fuel caches must remain outside tents and at least 20 feet away from open flames or active cook sites (p. 61).
8a(3).socratic_question: How far from your patrol cooking area and tents should extra fuel containers sit, and why is shade required?

9b(1).fact: The requirement demands climbing at least one thousand net vertical feet from the trailhead to the summit or turnaround point.
9b(1).misconception: Hiking four miles along a rolling mountain ridge fulfills the vertical gain requirement as long as the trail sits at high altitude.
9b(1).pamphlet_summary: Fulfilling this challenge requires calculating elevation difference using topographic contour lines rather than total trail distance. Hikers pace their ascent using the rest step technique and pack extra layers to handle rapid temperature drops on high ridges (p. 75).
9b(1).socratic_question: How can you use the index contour lines on a topographic map to verify that your route gains at least one thousand vertical feet?

9b(2).fact: The trek must occur as a continuous four-mile journey across wilderness terrain while carrying trail gear.
9b(2).misconception: Dividing four miles across short day strolls over several campouts satisfies this backcountry trek requirement.
9b(2).pamphlet_summary: Scouts complete a minimum four-mile journey carrying wilderness gear across backcountry terrain using backpacks, snowshoes, or cross-country skis. Proper pack adjustment centers the heaviest items close to the back and maintains a group pace suited to the slowest traveler (p. 77).
9b(2).socratic_question: Where should you place heavy items inside your backpack to preserve balance when navigating uneven trails or deep snow?

9b(3).fact: The bicycle trip requires a planned touring route covering fifteen continuous miles or four active hours with appropriate route navigation and trail tools.
9b(3).misconception: Riding a bicycle around a paved campground loop for several short intervals counts toward the touring trip requirement.
9b(3).pamphlet_summary: Cyclists must complete a fifteen-mile or four-hour ride while wearing an approved bicycle helmet and obeying local traffic laws. Conducting an air, brakes, and chain inspection before departure ensures mechanical reliability on distance routes (p. 79).
9b(3).socratic_question: What mechanical checks on your tires, brakes, and chain should you conduct before rolling out on a fifteen-mile ride?

9b(4).fact: BSA Safety Afloat rules require every person aboard a nonmotorized craft to wear a securely fastened life jacket at all times on the water.
9b(4).misconception: Sitting inside a canoe or kayak without fastening a life jacket is acceptable on calm lakes during mild summer weather.
9b(4).pamphlet_summary: Paddlers complete a water excursion of at least five miles or four hours in canoes, kayaks, rowboats, or rafts under BSA Safety Afloat guidelines. Every participant must wear a properly fitted Type III life jacket and pack expedition gear in lashed dry bags (p. 81).
9b(4).socratic_question: How do you determine whether a life jacket fits properly before launching a canoe or kayak?

9b(5).fact: Wearing tight, damp layers restricts blood circulation and traps perspiration, which causes rapid body cooling inside a sleeping bag.
9b(5).misconception: Wearing all available daytime clothing inside a sleeping bag keeps a camper warmest during subfreezing nights.
9b(5).pamphlet_summary: Snow camping requires erecting a winter-rated tent or constructing an insulated snow shelter such as a quinzee or snow trench. Campers place a closed-cell foam pad beneath an inflatable mattress to stop ground conduction and ventilate shelters to prevent moisture buildup (p. 83).
9b(5).socratic_question: Why is a closed-cell foam pad beneath your air mattress essential for sleeping on packed snow?

9b(6).fact: Scouting America climbing standards mandate a separate belay system managed by a qualified instructor to arrest any uncontrolled fall.
9b(6).misconception: Holding the rappel brake line tightly eliminates the need for an independent safety belay line during a descent.
9b(6).pamphlet_summary: Scouts descend a designated thirty-foot vertical rock or tower face using approved climbing webbing, harnesses, and friction devices under direct adult supervision. BSA policy mandates an independent top-rope belay system operated by a trained instructor to protect the rappeller (p. 85).
9b(6).socratic_question: Why must a secondary belay line protect you even when you have full control of your friction device?
